products.scene_director.guides.image_to_: How to Build Better Image-to-Image Prompts | URSUS Loft
Learn how to organize reference images, character details, camera direction, environment, and final instructions into a clearer image-to-image prompt workflow.
How to build clearer image-to-image prompts
A practical workflow for separating references, creative direction, and final instructions before you use an external image-generation service.

An image-to-image prompt combines written direction with one or more references. The written part explains what to preserve, what to change, and what kind of image you are trying to make. A useful prompt is not simply longer; it makes the relationship between instructions easier to understand.

Decide whether the goal is a character reference, a scene recreation, or a cinematic composition. That decision helps determine which details are essential and which should stay secondary. Write the result you need before collecting extra descriptive phrases.

Give each reference a job. One image may establish identity, another can support costume, and another can describe environment or pose. Keeping identity separate from costume and environment makes it easier to notice when two sources disagree.

Describe shot size, lens, camera height, angle, framing, and composition as their own direction. Camera choices affect how a subject appears, so they should not be buried inside identity or costume notes.

Check for incompatible viewpoints, body descriptions, lighting, or scenes. When priorities are clear, remove or rewrite details that compete with the intended result. An external image-generation service may still interpret the same prompt differently, so compare results by changing one controlled detail at a time.
Keep identity, costume, and environment distinct.
How Scene Director supports this workflow

Scene Director organizes reference roles, scene controls, and Final Prompt or Compact Prompt output in one Windows workspace. It prepares English prompt text; you use that text and upload the chosen references in an external service.

products.scene_director.guides.reference: Why Reference Image Order Matters in AI Image Generation | URSUS Loft
Learn how reference image order and role assignment affect structured image-to-image prompts and how to keep the same images in the same sequence.
Keep role assignments and image sequence visible when you move from prompt preparation to an external generation workflow.
Reference images can communicate face, body, costume, environment, pose, or rendering direction. Assigning a role makes it clear which image supports each instruction.
Keep the same images in the same sequence

When a prompt refers to image order, upload the same selected images in that order to the external service. This is a workflow principle, not a claim that every service interprets images in exactly the same way.
Do not invent a role for an empty slot. In Scene Director, empty slots and Role Required images are excluded from prompt output. Check what is included before copying a prompt.
Changing order after writing the prompt, replacing an image without reviewing its role, and using conflicting identity sources make a workflow harder to check.
Confirm each selected image has a purpose.
Upload the same images in the same sequence.
How Scene Director keeps order visible
Scene Director shows up to five reference slots and assigned roles while you build a Final Prompt or Compact Prompt. The app does not upload images; you attach them in the external workflow.

products.scene_director.guides.character: How to Improve Character Consistency in AI Image Generation | URSUS Loft
Use clearer reference roles and structured prompts to reduce conflicting identity, body, costume, pose, and camera instructions in AI image generation.
How to improve character consistency with clearer prompts
Use stable identity references and separate direction to reduce conflicts while working across scenes and compositions.

Character consistency is the effort to keep recognisable identity details coherent while scenes, poses, costumes, and camera choices change. References, prompt structure, and the external service all affect the result.
Choose a clear identity source and explain its role. If face, body, and costume come from different references, keep those roles separate instead of letting every image compete as general identity.
Use only the references that serve the requested result. Conflicting identity sources make it harder to review what should be preserved.
Camera and composition change presentation, not identity. Keep shot size, angle, lens, and framing in their own direction so they do not obscure identity details.
Keep identity instructions stable and change environment, action, and camera as separate layers. This makes recurring character work easier to review.
An external image-generation service interprets references and prompt text, so structured instructions support review but do not guarantee a specific result.
Separate face, body, and costume roles.
